cards.title: Training a model by making it criticise itself
cards.hook: The human's job shrinks from ranking thousands of harmful answers to writing down the rules. Then the model does the ranking.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Some of Claude's principles came from Apple's terms of service
cards.hook: Human-rights law has nothing to say about impersonating someone in a chat window. A phone company's terms of service do.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The alignment problem, stated in 1960
cards.hook: The alignment problem was stated in Science magazine in 1960, in one sentence, by the man who named cybernetics.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: You cannot write down what you want
cards.hook: The worry is not that a machine will disobey you. It is that it will obey, exactly, the thing you managed to write down.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: A Bank of England adviser named your AI's failure mode
cards.hook: The law that explains why your reward function breaks was written about the Bank of England's money-supply targets in 1975.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Credited Keith Hoskin for the 'when a measure becomes a target' phrasing that Strathern's 1997 paper carries.

cards.title: There is a public list of every way an optimiser cheated
cards.hook: Researchers keep a shared catalogue of every documented case of an optimiser finding the loophole. It runs to dozens.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: El barco que descubrió que la carrera no era el punto
cards.hook: El agente sacó más puntos que cualquier humano. También se incendió, chocó contra otras lanchas y jamás terminó la carrera.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: How do you grade an answer you cannot check?
cards.hook: Economics has a century of theory for hiring someone who knows more than you. All of it assumes you can eventually check the work.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The arithmetic behind every "we trained a big model"
cards.hook: Six operations per parameter per token. That single number turns any press release about a big model into a napkin calculation.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Recall distractor claimed 2ND = 1.4e23; 2ND is 2.8e23. Fixed that and the second distractor's non-teaching reason.

cards.title: Why a model is slow even on a very fast chip
cards.hook: While a model writes you a sentence, the fastest chip in the building is mostly idle, waiting for numbers to arrive.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Why AI labs have such strange corporate structures
cards.hook: A charity cannot raise a billion dollars for chips. A normal company cannot credibly promise to stop. Every lab is an attempt to be both.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Where the handful of frontier labs came from
cards.hook: "Frontier lab" is not a compliment. It names the handful of organisations that can afford the largest training runs.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Opened on a list of founding dates; moved the idea to the first line so the card leads with a claim rather than a roll call.

cards.title: Open weights is not open source, and the gap is enormous
cards.hook: Weights are the output of the build, not the build. You can run the model and change it; you can never check how it was made.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: You run the lab. Do you publish the weights?
cards.hook: The release decision that actually gets made is not "is this dangerous?". Everything is dangerous. Here is the question that replaces it.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Regulation had to pick a number, so it picked a big one
cards.hook: How do you legislate a technology you cannot define? You regulate the electricity bill instead.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: There is no AI regulator, and that is the point
cards.hook: Most of what people want from AI regulation is already illegal. The interesting question is who enforces it.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The transformer was published as a translation result
cards.hook: No language model appears anywhere in the abstract. The headline result is a German translation score.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The architecture that won by deleting something
cards.hook: The most consequential architecture of the decade was defined by what its authors threw out.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Backprop was invented at least three times before 1986
cards.hook: The algorithm behind every neural network was published in 1970, in Finnish, in a thesis about rounding errors.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The program that proved 38 theorems and got rejected anyway
cards.hook: It found a proof shorter than Whitehead and Russell's, and a journal declined the paper because one author was a program.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Two months, ten men, and the word that stuck
cards.hook: The field of artificial intelligence got its name inside a grant application, and the budget was two months.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The unfashionable idea that made deep learning work
cards.hook: The paper that cracked computer vision was a poster. What made it possible was years of paying strangers to label photographs.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Two gaming cards, six days, and vision fell over
cards.hook: Eleven percentage points is not an improvement. It is a change of era, and it arrived on two consumer graphics cards.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Swapped the NeurIPS abstract page for the PDF: only the PDF carries the 15.3%/26.2% sentence. Hook and body now agree on the 10.9-point gap.

cards.title: La máquina que ganó y a la que nunca le pidieron revancha
cards.hook: Deep Blue ganó sin aprender nada. Buscaba 200 millones de posiciones por segundo y evaluaba con reglas escritas a mano.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Remember why Go was supposed to be safe from computers?
cards.hook: Chess fell in 1997. Go held out until 2016. The gap is not nineteen years of hardware — it is one missing function.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The Navy announced a machine that would be conscious of its existence
cards.hook: In 1958 the US Navy told reporters it had the embryo of a computer that would one day be conscious of its existence.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: The convergence theorem was proved in 1962 (Rosenblatt's book, Novikoff independently), not before the 1958 press release. Dated it.

cards.title: The book everyone blames for the first neural-network winter
cards.hook: They were classmates at the same high school. One wrote the book that is blamed for burying the other's life's work.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: The 'sterile' verdict is the 1969 book's own conjecture, not a fresh 1988 judgement; rewrote that sentence. The 1988 edition reprinted the text with a new prologue and epilogue, no retraction.

cards.title: What Minsky and Papert actually proved
cards.hook: Everyone says the 1969 book proved a perceptron can't do XOR. XOR was the easy part and everyone already knew it.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Added a related link to the neural-nets XOR card, which shares the impossibility proof.

cards.title: The Turing test began as a game about telling men from women
cards.hook: Before a machine was allowed into it, Turing's test was a parlour game about telling a man from a woman.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Turing thought his own question was meaningless
cards.hook: Turing opened the founding paper of AI with a question, then threw the question away.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: One report, and British AI lost its funding
cards.hook: A fluid dynamicist was asked to review AI in 1973. British AI research did not recover for a decade.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Cut the unsupported 'they lost' about the 1973 BBC debate; the verifiable outcome is the funding withdrawal, which is what the sentence now carries.

cards.title: The second AI boom died of maintenance
cards.hook: An expert system saved one company an estimated 25 million dollars a year. Five years later the whole industry was gone.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The two-head circuit that finishes a pattern you just showed it
cards.hook: Look back for the last time this token appeared, take whatever came next, predict that. A whole mechanism, located and verified.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember inner products? Almost-perpendicular is nearly as good
cards.hook: Exactly perpendicular gives you n directions. Nearly perpendicular gives you exponentially many.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: How many separate ideas fit in 512 dimensions?
cards.hook: 512 numbers per token, and a few thousand things worth tracking. Something has to give.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: One neuron for cat faces and car fronts, and that is not a bug
cards.hook: A neuron that fires for Arabic script, DNA and base64 is not confused. It is sharing.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: If a probe finds a concept, did the network have it or did you build it?
cards.hook: A probe that recovers verb tense from the activations will also recover a property you invented at random.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: If the features hide between the neurons, build a dictionary
cards.hook: Stop reading neurons. Learn 4,096 sparse directions out of 512 of them and read those instead.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: They turned one feature up and the model thought it was a bridge
cards.hook: They found the feature by watching what it responds to, and proved it by turning it up.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: A calculator is just more tokens
cards.hook: A 1974 pocket calculator multiplies better than any language model. Getting one into the model costs no new architecture at all.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Attention is an average where the model picks the weights
cards.hook: Attention has a reputation for being mysterious. It is an average — the model just gets to pick the weights.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: One average was not enough, so they ran eight
cards.hook: One average per layer would be a poor machine. The 2017 model ran eight at once, and it cost nothing extra.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Remember inner products? Attention drops the symmetry axiom
cards.hook: An inner product is symmetric by axiom. Attention uses one that is not — and the asymmetry is the whole point.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Your context window just doubled. What did that cost?
cards.hook: Your context window goes from 8k to 16k tokens. Two resources change, and they do not change by the same factor.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the KV-cache idea card in the same topic; this is its puzzle form.

cards.title: Why the first token is slow and the rest just stream
cards.hook: The pause before the first word and the smooth stream afterwards are two different computations, and one is quadratic.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the KV-cache challenge card in the same topic.

cards.title: The jump might have been in the ruler
cards.hook: Scores that sit at zero for three orders of magnitude and then leap. Either capability arrives suddenly, or the ruler has a cliff in it.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The exam was already in the training set
cards.hook: Every benchmark old enough to be trusted is old enough to be on the web. The model has probably read the answer key.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Por qué te inventa la bibliografía con tanta seguridad
cards.hook: Autores reales, revista real, año verosímil, volumen y páginas. Y el artículo no existe. No es un error del modelo: es su objetivo.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Rioplatense voseo (pedis, descompone, vos no tenes) replaced with the Colombian reader's usage.

cards.title: Learning that leaves no trace
cards.hook: Show it three examples and it does the task. Clear the window and it has no idea it ever could.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The examples in your prompt can be wrong and it hardly matters
cards.hook: Replace every label in your examples with a random one. Performance barely moves. So what were the examples doing?
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The most likely sentence is one nobody would write
cards.hook: Train a model to put high probability on real text. Then ask it for the highest-probability text and you get a loop.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The temperature knob is Boltzmann's
cards.hook: The temperature setting is not a metaphor borrowed from physics. It is the same formula, with the same letter.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: A trillion parameters, most of them asleep
cards.hook: Most networks run every parameter on every input. Nobody made them. Turn that off and capacity stops costing compute.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: A picture is worth 196 tokens
cards.hook: Chop the photo into 196 squares, call each one a word, and feed it to the same machine that reads text. It works.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Every position in the document is its own exam question
cards.hook: A thousand-word document is not one training example. It is a thousand.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: One objective, repeated a few trillion times
cards.hook: The whole objective is: cover the next word, guess it, get told the answer. Repeat a few trillion times.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Remember entropy? It is the number on a model's report card
cards.hook: A model's training loss is not an arbitrary score. It is measured in bits, and it has a floor nobody can go below.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Position as a rotation, not an addition
cards.hook: Don't add position to the vector. Turn the vector. Then only the angle between two tokens survives the dot product.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Added the missing prerequisites (attention, inner products) for a difficulty-4 card.

cards.title: Remember Fourier? Position is written in sines and cosines
cards.hook: Attention cannot tell a sentence from its own shuffled anagram. The 2017 fix was to hand every position a Fourier expansion.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Eight worked examples took it from 18% to 57%
cards.hook: Same model, same eight example problems. Show the working in the examples and the score goes from 18% to 57%.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The working it shows is not the working it did
cards.hook: Reorder the options so the answer is always (A). The model follows the pattern — and writes a confident explanation that never mentions it.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Stop making it memorise and hand it the book
cards.hook: A model's knowledge is smeared across billions of weights. You cannot look it up, cannot edit it, cannot cite it.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The reward model is a 1952 paper about paired comparisons
cards.hook: The statistical core of modern preference training is a 1952 Biometrika paper on ranking things from incomplete tournaments.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 4 to 3: Bradley-Terry by maximum likelihood sits inside this reader's econometrics, not above it.

cards.title: Predicting text and answering a person are different jobs
cards.hook: A raw pretrained model asked a question will often reply with more questions. It is not being difficult — it is predicting.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: A hundred times smaller and better company
cards.hook: A hundredfold difference in size, and the small one won the human vote.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The graph that turned model-building into budgeting
cards.hook: Almost nothing in science stays on the same straight line for seven orders of magnitude. The loss of a language model does.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Everyone had been building the wrong shape
cards.hook: For three years everybody built models too big and fed them too little. 400 experiments in 2022 showed the whole field the same mistake.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Verified Table 3 (20.2 tokens/parameter at 1B, 20.5 at 10B) and MMLU 67.6% against Table 6; the abstract prints 67.5%. Both figures stand as written.

cards.title: Your budget just went up tenfold. What do you buy?
cards.hook: Your compute budget just went up tenfold. Spend it wrong and you burn it on the wrong-shaped model.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the Chinchilla idea card in the same topic; this is its puzzle form.

cards.title: A file-shrinking trick from 1994 became the alphabet of chatbots
cards.hook: The alphabet every chatbot reads in was designed in 1994 to shrink files, by a man who was not thinking about language.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: El mismo texto, en español, sale más caro
cards.hook: El mismo párrafo, traducido, puede costar el triple. El tokenizador cobra por pedazo, y no todos los idiomas se parten igual.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The model has never seen a letter
cards.hook: A language model has never seen a letter. Before it reads anything, your sentence has already been shredded.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The original transformer trained in twelve hours
cards.hook: The architecture behind every large language model was introduced by a model small enough to fit on a phone.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Nothing gets replaced; everything gets added
cards.hook: Nothing in a transformer replaces anything. Every layer reads a running total and adds to it.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The famous part is the small part
cards.hook: The paper was called Attention Is All You Need. Two thirds of the weights are in the part that never looks at another word.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Derive the tradeoff, then find where it stops being a law
cards.hook: Four lines of algebra give bias² + variance + noise. Nothing in those lines says the two must trade off.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Two completely different ways for a model to be wrong
cards.hook: One model is wrong the same way every time. Another is wrong differently every time. The cures are opposite.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Diagram caption: bias and variance 'move separately' rather than 'are independent of each other'.

cards.title: k-means always finds k clusters, even when there are none
cards.hook: Hand it one featureless blob and ask for four groups. It will give you four groups, without embarrassment.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: A test set you look at twice is a training set
cards.hook: Every decision you make after peeking at held-out data spends a little of it. Leaderboards spend a lot.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Los mapas de t-SNE mienten, y mienten de forma predecible
cards.hook: El tamaño de los grupos no significa nada. La distancia entre grupos tampoco. Algo sí significa, y conviene saber qué.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember the SVD? PCA is the SVD wearing a lab coat
cards.hook: You already proved the theorem. PCA is what it looks like when the matrix happens to be a data table.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: A gradient from 32 examples beats a gradient from a million
cards.hook: The exact gradient costs a full pass over your data and buys one step. A sloppy one buys thousands.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Gradient descent is older than the light bulb
cards.hook: 1847: a two-page note to the French Academy, written to chase orbits, not neurons.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: How to compute in a million dimensions without going there
cards.hook: The algorithm never touches the expanded features. It only ever asks for inner products between pairs.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Of all the lines that separate them, take the one with room to spare
cards.hook: Infinitely many lines separate the two clouds. One is the middle of the widest street you can drive between them.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: "Linear" is a claim about the parameters, not about the world
cards.hook: A linear model can fit a wave, a circle or a step function. 'Linear' was never a claim about the inputs.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The first model fitted to data was hunting a lost planet
cards.hook: A 24-year-old fitted a curve to 41 days of measurements and told astronomers where to point. They found it.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Accuracy is the number you want and the worst thing to optimise
cards.hook: A cancer test that answers 'no' to everyone is 99% accurate. That is the mild problem with accuracy.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Choose a loss and you have quietly chosen a probability model
cards.hook: Squared error is not a neutral default. It is an assumption about your noise, wearing a disguise.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Memorizar el simulacro no es estudiar
cards.hook: Sacar 100 en los simulacros es una pésima noticia si lo que memorizaste fueron los simulacros.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Ridge and lasso are opinions about the world, written as penalties
cards.hook: Add a penalty to your loss and you have not 'regularised'. You have stated a prior and taken its mode.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The unsupervised revolution was supervised all along
cards.hook: Nobody labelled the internet — so the objective quietly stole its labels from the text itself.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Somebody had to write down the right answers
cards.hook: Photographs are free. Photographs labelled 'golden retriever' cost money — so the field learned to manufacture labels.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The statistician who told statistics it was 2% of the story
cards.hook: He put his own colleagues at 98% of the profession, and said they were answering the wrong question.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: A forest beats a tree because the trees disagree
cards.hook: Average five hundred identical trees and you get one tree. The whole engineering problem is making them differ.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Every learner is a bet about what the world looks like
cards.hook: Two models fit your data perfectly and disagree everywhere else. Something other than the data breaks the tie.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Mitchell 1997 now links to the book's own page rather than the author's Wikipedia entry.

cards.title: A lookup table is not learning, and that gap is the whole subject
cards.hook: Store every answer you have ever seen and you score 100% on the past and nothing at all on the future.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Mitchell 1997 now links to the book's own page rather than the author's Wikipedia entry.

cards.title: Remember uniform convergence? It is what "universal approximation" means
cards.hook: One hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a box. The theorem says nothing about how wide, and that is the point.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The kink that beat the S-curve
cards.hook: The standard unit squashed everything into a smooth S. Its derivative never exceeds one quarter, and that turned out to be fatal.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: How to differentiate through a coin flip
cards.hook: You need the derivative of an expectation whose distribution you are learning. Sampling has no derivative. Move the randomness.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Learning by being forced to forget
cards.hook: Train a network to copy its input to its output. Absurd — until you make the middle too narrow for a copy to fit.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Every derivative for the price of one forward pass
cards.hook: Nudging each parameter to see what happens would take a hundred billion forward passes. The real cost is about two.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Remember Hebb's rule? Backprop has the same shape and the opposite politics
cards.hook: Hebb's rule needs nothing but the two cells it joins. Backprop needs a number computed at the far end of the network.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Named Siegrid Lowel (1992) as the source of the fire-together-wire-together paraphrase.

cards.title: Nature, 9 October 1986
cards.hook: Two sentences from 1986 still describe, completely, how every model you have heard of was trained.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: La misma ventanita, repetida en todas partes
cards.hook: Una capa densa sobre una foto necesita cien millones de pesos. Un filtro de nueve números hace más, porque se repite.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Rioplatense imperatives (pone, gira) replaced with the Colombian reader's usage.

cards.title: The cell that ignored every dot and woke up for an edge
cards.hook: They spent hours showing a cat dots of light and got nothing. The cell woke up for the shadow of a glass slide.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Remember Brownian motion? Now run it backwards
cards.hook: A random walk forgets where it started. Diffusion models are the claim that you can teach a network to remember.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Train it only to remove noise, and out comes a painter
cards.hook: The training task is a homework exercise: guess what noise was added. Do it at every noise level and you get a machine that invents images.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: A word stops being a name and becomes a direction
cards.hook: The only thing a model can do with the number 4842 is use it as a row index. That row is where meaning starts.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Remember the angle between vectors? It became the definition of "similar"
cards.hook: Two random directions in a thousand dimensions are almost exactly perpendicular. That is why a cosine of 0.3 means something.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Two networks, and one of them is lying
cards.hook: The generator never sees a real image. Its only information about reality is how badly it fooled a critic.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Fifty-six layers lost to twenty, on the training set
cards.hook: The deeper network did worse on the training set. Not overfitting — it could not even fit.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Every parameter gets its own step size
cards.hook: One learning rate has to be small enough for the loudest parameter, which means the quietest one never moves at all.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: A neuron is a dot product and a kink
cards.hook: Strip away the biology and a neuron is two operations: an inner product, and a bend. The bend is the whole reason depth exists.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 1 to 2: the rigor counts regions of a hyperplane arrangement, which is not a level-1 ask.

cards.title: Four points that no straight line can separate
cards.hook: Four points, two labels, and no straight line that separates them. One hidden layer with two units settles it in a page.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the Perceptrons history card, which shares the XOR impossibility proof.

cards.title: Insufficient, decaying error back flow
cards.hook: The 1997 paper that ran translation and speech for two decades opens by naming its enemy in one phrase.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: The gradient that dies on the way back
cards.hook: A recurrent network is a deep network where every layer is the same layer. Multiply one matrix by itself forty times and see what survives.
cards.author: author-ai-llm-1

cards.title: Search that decides for itself where to look
cards.hook: Every node of the search tree is a slot machine. That one idea turns an impossible search into a practical one.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The move no human would have played
cards.hook: AlphaGo's own model of human play said one professional in ten thousand would make that move. It made it anyway.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: The one-in-ten-thousand figure is David Silver's recollection, not in the Nature paper; the card now says so. Dropped the unsourced 'left the room' detail for what commentary records.

cards.title: A doctor with two treatments and no way to be fair
cards.hook: Every patient you give the worse treatment to is a cost. Every patient you give the untested one to is information. You cannot have both.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: The restaurant problem you solve badly every week
cards.hook: Simon said you satisfice because optimising costs more than it is worth. The bandit maths says satisficing costs you linearly, forever.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: This feed is running a bandit on you right now
cards.hook: The card you are reading was chosen by a slot machine with one arm per topic. Here is the machine.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Checked against ENGINE.md 6: Beta(1,1) arms, a += r, kappa = 4, gamma = 0.985/day all correct. Added that the Thompson draw is one factor in the score, not the argmax.

cards.title: A Markov chain with a steering wheel
cards.hook: A Markov chain tells you where you will end up. Add one choice per state and it tells you where you can make yourself end up.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: He named it "dynamic programming" to get it past Washington
cards.hook: It is not dynamic and it is not programming. Bellman picked the name so that nobody could defund it.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Flagged the hole in Bellman's memoir: Wilson only became Secretary of Defense in 1953, three years after the naming.

cards.title: When your choices change the board
cards.hook: A slot machine forgets you. A chess board does not. The moment your action changes what you face next, the problem changes shape.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Differentiating through luck
cards.hook: You cannot differentiate a dice roll. The log-derivative trick moves the derivative onto the dice instead.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: It learned a backflip from 900 yes-or-no answers
cards.hook: Nobody can write a reward function for 'do a backflip'. So they didn't, and asked a human 900 times which clip looked better.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Added OpenAI's write-up as a source: the 900 comparisons and the backflip are in the paper body and that post, not in the abstract.

cards.title: Learning the value of a move you didn't make
cards.hook: You can behave badly on purpose and still learn what the best behaviour is worth. That is the strangest property in reinforcement learning.
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Two slot machines that pay nothing. Which looks better?
cards.hook: Two machines, both worth exactly zero. Estimate each from one noisy pull, report the bigger number. Are you right on average?
cards.author: author-ai-history-1

cards.title: Fitting the noise exactly, and getting away with it
cards.hook: There are infinitely many ways to interpolate. Gradient descent picks one, and that choice is the entire story.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember singular values? They decide whether overfitting kills you
cards.hook: Inverting a matrix with one tiny singular value destroys a computation. It also explains the whole double-descent peak.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: More data can make your model worse, and the graph shows where
cards.hook: Same model, more training data, worse test error. The peak does not care which axis you walk in on.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Opening now follows episode 3 instead of assuming the reader has already met the curve.

cards.title: You have 100 points and you keep adding features. Predict the curve.
cards.hook: Ten lines of code, one plot, and the shape every statistics course teaches is wrong about two-thirds of it.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Softened an unverifiable claim about what most statistics graduates answer.

cards.title: The curve that isn't supposed to exist
cards.hook: Classical theory says the worst model size is the one that fits the data perfectly. Go bigger and the error falls again.
cards.author: lead

cards.title: The honest bound for a real network says "error at most 400%"
cards.hook: Plug a real network's parameter count into the classical theorem and it guarantees nothing. Not approximately nothing.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Numbers now match the title and episode 1: 10^6 weights on 5x10^4 images gives ~4.5, 14 at 10^7; added the Bartlett et al. lower bound.

cards.title: They replaced every label with a coin flip. The network learned it anyway.
cards.hook: If a network can memorise pure noise, then nothing about its architecture can explain why it generalises.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The network memorised the answer, then understood it much later
cards.hook: Training accuracy hit 100% and validation stayed at chance. They left it running. Two orders of magnitude later it understood.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Reverse-engineer a grokked network and you find trigonometry
cards.hook: It learned modular addition by rotating around a circle. The algorithm is sitting in the weights, in Fourier space.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Nobody wrote the regulariser. The optimiser is the regulariser.
cards.hook: Keep training after the loss is already tiny and the classifier keeps moving — toward the maximum margin, logarithmically slowly.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Stopping early is ridge regression, with the step count as lambda
cards.hook: Nobody added a penalty. Cutting training short adds one anyway, and you can compute its strength.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The claim that networks learn by forgetting, and the fight about it
cards.hook: Tishby said training has two phases: fit, then forget. Then somebody re-ran it with a different activation function.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: In a million dimensions, getting stuck is not what goes wrong
cards.hook: For a point to be a local minimum, a million curvatures must all come out positive. The odds are poor.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The one-line fix that made lottery tickets work on real networks
cards.hook: The lottery is not drawn at initialisation. It is drawn a few hundred steps in, once the run has chosen a basin.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: The linear-interpolation error barrier is from Frankle et al. 2020 (arXiv:1912.05671), not the 2019 paper; source added and the stability claim corrected.

cards.title: A random network already contains the network you were going to train
cards.hook: Not 'a subnetwork that trains well' — a subnetwork that is already the answer, at its random initial weights.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Delete 90% of the network, rewind the survivors, and it still works
cards.hook: The same sparse network trains well from its original random numbers and fails from fresh ones. Same shape, different luck.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Dated the work 2018 (arXiv) with the ICLR 2019 best-paper award, instead of 2019.

cards.title: A theory costing more bits than the data explains nothing
cards.hook: Compression is not a metaphor for learning. Under a fixed code, they are literally the same optimisation.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember the halting problem? It rules out the perfect learner
cards.hook: The perfect inductive method exists, is provably optimal, and provably cannot be run.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember Gödel? Learning theory has its own "no system does everything"
cards.hook: Two theorems that kill a universal object, and two fields that carried on by naming their assumptions instead.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Qualified no free lunch: all algorithms share the same expected off-training error, which is 1/2 for binary labels under 0-1 loss.

cards.title: No hay almuerzo gratis: ningún algoritmo le gana a los demás
cards.hook: Promediado sobre todos los mundos posibles, tu mejor modelo empata con lanzar una moneda. La trampa está en 'todos'.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Make a network infinitely wide and it turns into a kernel machine
cards.hook: In the wide limit the weights barely move, the network becomes its own linearisation, and training turns into kernel regression.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Remember Hoeffding? That inequality is the whole theory of learning
cards.hook: An inequality about coin flips, plus one counting trick, is most of the reason machine learning works.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: What the theory actually promised: probably, approximately, right
cards.hook: The theory never promised the truth. It promised a bound on how often you are badly wrong — and that bound is cheap.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

reviewed.notes: Recall fixed: confidence costs about 7/epsilon extra examples (additive), not 'a constant multiple'.

cards.title: Measure a model's capacity by asking it to fit coin flips
cards.hook: The random-label experiment, turned into a definition — and published fifteen years earlier.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: The right way to measure capacity is a game played with points
cards.hook: Three points in the plane: a line can produce all eight colourings. Four points: never all sixteen.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: One real parameter is enough for infinite capacity
cards.hook: One real number, and the class shatters any finite set you name.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Past the VC dimension, exponential growth turns polynomial
cards.hook: Infinitely many functions can behave in at most n^d ways on n points. That collapse is the whole theorem.
cards.author: author-ai-theory-1

cards.title: Cancer incidence rises as about the fifth power of your age
cards.hook: Plot cancer incidence against age on log paper and you get a straight line of slope five. That slope is a count of something.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Source was misattributed: the 2007 Lancet Oncology "Armitage and Doll revisited" paper is by Hornsby, Page and Tomlinson, not by Armitage and Doll. Fixed author and citation.

cards.title: They signed away insulin for a dollar each
cards.hook: Three men signed away the insulin patent for a dollar each. The quote everybody attaches to that story appears to be invented.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember counting arrangements? Your immune system does it for a living
cards.hook: A few dozen gene segments, cut and pasted at random, generate more receptor shapes than there are cells in your body.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: You are not outnumbered ten to one
cards.hook: "Ten bacterial cells for every human cell" was a back-of-envelope guess from 1972 that ran unchallenged for forty years.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The kitchen blender that proved genes are made of DNA
cards.hook: A kitchen blender and two radioactive labels finally ended an argument the field had been refusing to settle for eight years.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Added the Avery 1944 caveat — Hershey-Chase persuaded the field rather than settling the question from scratch.

cards.title: Two metres of thread in a six-micron room, and it never knots
cards.hook: Twenty kilometres of fishing line in a tennis ball — copied and pulled apart without a knot, every time a cell divides.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember that energy is conserved but not free? Cells built a dam
cards.hook: You already know energy is conserved but not free. Your cells turn that into a dam, a waterfall and a spinning turbine.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Cyanobacteria have no chloroplasts: the c14 ring is the plant chloroplast one. Named the ring sizes (8 and 14) that give the 2.7 and 4.7 ratios.

cards.title: Every cell you own holds back a lightning-strength field
cards.hook: Seventy millivolts across five nanometres is a field several times stronger than the one that turns air into a spark.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: The pump does not itself hold the inside negative: named the potassium leak that actually produces the voltage, since "the pump makes the -70 mV" is a standard misconception.

cards.title: The paper that fifteen journals did not want
cards.hook: About fifteen journals turned the paper down. It said the powerhouses inside your cells used to be free-living bacteria.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Bacteria count themselves, and they refuse to glow until the vote passes
cards.hook: A single bacterium never glows. Put ten billion of them in a squid's light organ and they all switch on at once.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Repaired a broken sentence in the rigor layer ("fall out that matching the intuition demands").

cards.title: 80.346 especies, y el número se mueve cuando cambia quien cuenta
cards.hook: 80.346 especies registradas al cierre de 2024. La cifra dice tanto sobre la biología del país como sobre quién se puso a contar.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Cut unverified counts (1,966 birds; 8,500 endemics) and the "cierra cada 31 de diciembre" framing. Kept SiB's verified December-2024 figures and added the 4th-place methodology point, which is the card's thesis.

cards.title: El dibujo que bajó del Chimborazo
cards.hook: Humboldt subió el Chimborazo en 1802 y bajó con un dibujo. Ese dibujo fundó la biogeografía.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Bogotá bebe de una planta peluda
cards.hook: Colombia tiene cerca de la mitad de los páramos del mundo, y 17 millones de personas toman agua que pasó primero por hojas peludas.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Removed the unsourced "16 ciudades" and an unverifiable frailejon growth range; kept the verified Humboldt Institute figures (2.9 Mha, 36 complejos, 2.5%, 17 million people).

cards.title: How much grass is a lion?
cards.hook: Work out why nothing on land eats lions, using one number and two multiplications.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember phase portraits? Lynx and hares drew one
cards.hook: A century of fur-trade ledgers, two coupled ODEs, and closed orbits that never settle and never die.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Darwin looked at an orchid and ordered a moth
cards.hook: A flower with a foot-long nectar tube made Darwin predict an unseen moth. Nobody watched one drink from it for 135 years.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: The 1992 photographs and 2004 video are not documented; the published first record is Wasserthal 1997. Fixed body and hook, added the Wasserthal paper as a source.

cards.title: The envelope that ended twenty years of not publishing
cards.hook: Darwin sat on the idea for twenty years. It took one envelope from a Malay island to get him to publish.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Most of evolution is nobody's fault
cards.hook: Two lines of algebra in which the population size cancels out — and a clock appears with nothing ticking.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: A mouse gene, dropped into a fly, orders an eye
cards.hook: Switch a fly gene on in the wrong place and the fly grows an eye there. Switch on the mouse version and it works just as well.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember Nash equilibrium? Evolution found a stricter version
cards.hook: Nash assumed players who reason. Evolution has none, gets equilibrium anyway, and its version is strictly stronger.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Fixed callback.from (was econ.game-theory.evolutionary, which gates the card behind the idea it teaches) to dominance-nash; corrected "Nash equilibria are exactly the rest points" — the converse fails.

cards.title: A species that vanished 40,000 years ago is still inside you
cards.hook: Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago. If your ancestry runs outside Africa, roughly 2% of you is theirs.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The arithmetic of dying for your brother
cards.hook: Two brothers, or eight cousins. The arithmetic is real; the pub quote it is famous for probably is not.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember Darwin's three facts? That is a definition of learning
cards.hook: Variation, heredity, differential success. Rename the three and you have written down what 'learning' means in machine learning.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Three facts and one conclusion
cards.hook: Darwin's argument mentions no genes, no DNA, not even life. It is three observations and a conclusion that cannot be refused.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: He found a third kind of life by reading one molecule
cards.hook: In 1977 one molecule revealed a whole domain of life that nobody had noticed, and the field's reaction was to tell him to stop.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Added sources for the Luria and Mayr objections, which no cited source carried (three-domain system; Mayr 1998 PNAS).

cards.title: The feather that made Darwin sick
cards.hook: A peacock's tail is a survival disaster. Darwin said so in a letter, then spent eleven years explaining it.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: "Interbreeds with" is not transitive, and that is what a species is
cards.hook: Walk a ring of salamanders round a valley. Every neighbour interbreeds with the next, and the two ends will not.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Crick picked the wrong word, and biology kept it anyway
cards.hook: Crick admitted later that he did not know what 'dogma' meant when he named the most famous rule in biology.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Diagram caption called reverse transcription "the one real exception", contradicting the card's own rigor (three special transfers). Reworded.

cards.title: Bacteria keep a scrapbook of everyone who ever tried to kill them
cards.hook: The gene-editing tool of the decade started as an unexplained pattern of repeats next to a bacterial gene in 1987.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The most under-stated sentence in the history of biology
cards.hook: One page in Nature, two chains, four letters — and the most under-stated sentence anyone has written about heredity.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: A famine that ended in 1945, still legible in 2008
cards.hook: People conceived in the Dutch famine of 1944 carry a chemical difference sixty years on. The caveats matter as much as the result.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Two Frenchmen found an if-statement inside a bacterium
cards.hook: E. coli digests lactose only when there is lactose and no glucose. In 1961 two Frenchmen found the circuit that computes it.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The monk's peas saved an argument Darwin never knew was broken
cards.hook: If inheritance blended like paint, natural selection would run out of material in ten generations. Darwin never learned why it does not.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: How many typos did you start life with?
cards.hook: You were born carrying single-letter changes that neither of your parents had. Guess the order of magnitude before you read on.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The theorem that says nothing happens
cards.hook: A pure mathematician settled biology's loudest argument of 1908 with one line of algebra, and apologised for intruding.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Yule's objection is documented as dominants spreading until they swamp recessives; the brown-eyes/blue-eyes version is not in the cited sources. Hardy's opening quote verified verbatim.

cards.title: What did it cost to read one human genome in 2001?
cards.hook: One curve in biology outran Moore's law for years. Guess the numbers before you look.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Mendel's data are too good to be true
cards.hook: Fisher did not ask whether Mendel's peas fit the theory. He asked whether they fit it too well, and computed the odds.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Event date corrected to the paper's 15 April 1936. Fisher's "once in twenty-nine trials" and "falsified to agree closely" both verified verbatim via Hartl and Fairbanks 2007.

cards.title: One line that holds all of Darwin
cards.hook: An outsider with no training in genetics wrote one line that contains selection, transmission and Darwin's entire argument.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Price did not sell his house; he moved on a thyroid-surgery insurance payout in November 1967. Corrected, which also makes the story sharper.

cards.title: Photo 51, told properly
cards.hook: The famous X-ray was taken in May 1952. What Franklin had already worked out from it matters more than who showed it to whom.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: El médico que tenía razón veinte años antes
cards.hook: En 1881 Finlay dijo cuál mosquito transmitía la fiebre amarilla. Tuvieron que pasar casi veinte años para que le creyeran.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The word "cell" is not about monks
cards.hook: Hooke compared them to a honeycomb. The story about monks' rooms is a later invention that everyone repeats.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Leeuwenhoek's rainwater animalcules were 1676; the dental scrapings were 1683. Split the two dates. Monks'-cells myth confirmed against Peters 2024, Plant Cell 36(11).

cards.title: A jar of gas, a spark, and amino acids by Friday
cards.hook: A graduate student sealed four gases in glass, ran sparks through them for a week, and found the building blocks of protein.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The map of your body in your head has enormous lips
cards.hook: There is a map of your body in your cortex, and its hands and lips are grotesquely oversized. That distortion is the useful part.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Your brain may be running a test Wald wrote down in 1945
cards.hook: Wald's 1945 test for deciding when you have seen enough data has a candidate implementation in parietal cortex.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 2 to 3: the rigor is Wald's SPRT plus drift-diffusion first-passage closed forms, on a par with the other level-3 cards in the shard.

cards.title: Remember entropy? A fly's neuron carries about 90 bits a second
cards.hook: Entropy told you how much a message could say. Point it at a fly's spike train and you get a number: about 90 bits a second.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Dropped an unsupported claim (rates "double from 25 ms to sub-millisecond"): Strong et al. scan 800 ms to 2 ms, entropy rate rising ~40x at ~50% efficiency. 90 bits/s and 0.5-2 bits/spike verified.

cards.title: Everything we know about nerves, we learned from a squid
cards.hook: A squid grew a nerve fibre a thousand times fatter than yours, for reasons of its own. Neuroscience has been living off it ever since.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Four equations that make a nerve fire
cards.hook: Four coupled nonlinear ODEs, fitted in 1952, predicted the shape and the speed of a nerve impulse before anyone knew channels were proteins.
cards.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: HH's rest state is globally attracting, so the "threshold" is not a basin boundary. Replaced with FitzHugh's quasi-threshold, in the rigor and in the recall distractor.

cards.title: He got better at a task he swore he had never done
cards.hook: He improved at the task on every attempt, over days, while insisting each time that he had never attempted it.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Nobody knows why you sleep
cards.hook: A third of your life, unconscious and undefended. Evolution rarely pays a bill like that for nothing, and nobody knows what it buys.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: The experiment he had to dream twice
cards.hook: He dreamed the decisive experiment, woke, wrote it down, and in the morning could not read his own handwriting.
cards.author: author-bio-1

cards.title: Remember the folk theorem? Axelrod asked the question it can't answer
cards.hook: The folk theorem says cooperation can be an equilibrium. Axelrod asked a different question entirely.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The shortest program in the room won, twice
cards.hook: Fourteen game theorists submitted programs. The shortest one beat all of them, twice.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Cut 'three countries and five disciplines' (uncheckable); added an open source. Tournament tallies are Axelrod's own and internally consistent (15 rules x 120 pairings x 200 x 5 x 2 = 240,000).

cards.title: How do you falsify a world you built yourself?
cards.hook: The most celebrated validated simulation in the field matched a thousand years of history and still got the ending wrong.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Conway bet fifty dollars against his own game. He lost in a month.
cards.hook: Conway bet fifty dollars that nothing in his game could grow forever. He lost within weeks.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Hook said 'inside two months'; Gardner's column ran October 1970 and Gosper's gun arrived that November, so 'within weeks'.

cards.title: "Emergent" is not an answer. It's a receipt.
cards.hook: If a word explains everything it explains nothing. "Emergent" is one round from that.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Remember the Ising model? You have already seen Schelling's board
cards.hook: Magnets and neighbourhoods obey the same equation. One of them has a temperature; the other has tolerance.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Rigor used $u_i$ for both utility and unlike-neighbour count; rewritten with separate like/unlike counts.

cards.title: An epidemic stops long before it runs out of people
cards.hook: An epidemic does not stop when the virus runs out of people. It stops earlier, and you can say exactly when.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Three rules, and a cloud of bats over Gotham
cards.hook: The bat swarm in Batman Returns has no choreographer. It has three rules, written in 1986.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Ballerini et al. report six-seven neighbours, not 'roughly seven'.

cards.title: En Bogotá la segregación no tuvo que emerger: se decretó
cards.hook: El modelo de Schelling segrega sin que nadie lo ordene. Colombia lo ordena por ley, con seis números.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Want half your neighbours to match. You'll get four-fifths.
cards.hook: Schelling ran the first famous social simulation by hand, moving coins on graph paper one at a time.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Diagram caption claimed an equilibrium 'after 45 people move', which the figure does not show; recaptioned with the run's measured 53% -> 75%. Body numbers all check against Schelling pp. 155-159.

cards.title: They grew a society and it invented inequality
cards.hook: Two economists gave near-identical rules to near-identical agents and got a wealth distribution that looks like ours.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: "If you didn't grow it, you didn't explain it"
cards.hook: Nine words that set the entrance fee for an entire field — and that its author insists are not enough.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The model you have to run to find out what it says
cards.hook: An equation model tells you the answer. An agent-based model makes you watch.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: A jet engine is complicated. A city is complex.
cards.hook: In 1948 a Rockefeller Foundation director named the exact class of problems science could not yet touch.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: The Weaver source pointed at his Wikipedia biography, which never mentions the 1948 essay; repointed to the American Scientist article itself.

cards.title: The pile that tunes itself to the edge
cards.hook: A phase transition normally needs someone to set the temperature. Bak claimed some systems drive themselves there.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Twenty-four data sets went in. One power law came out.
cards.hook: Twenty-four famous data sets, tested properly. Exactly one came out convincingly power-law.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked to the scale-free networks card, which teaches the same lesson from a different study.

cards.title: The bar on Canyon Road that broke rational expectations
cards.hook: There is a real bar on Canyon Road in Santa Fe, and it has a theorem named after it.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Gell-Mann and Pines were not Los Alamos scientists; founders line corrected. Arthur 1994 source repointed from a wiki page to his own hosted PDF.

cards.title: One hundred people, one hundred thresholds
cards.hook: Two crowds with almost identical people. One riots, one goes home. Find the difference.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Remember the median voter? That theorem is your null model
cards.hook: The median voter theorem is a simulation with one agent in it. Adding a thousand only helps if you know which assumption you dropped.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Source repointed to arXiv v1, since the unversioned link now serves the retitled June 2026 version.

cards.title: Your simulated electorate votes. Now defend it.
cards.hook: The agents no longer follow rules you wrote. So what is left to check?
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Source repointed to arXiv v1, since the unversioned link now serves the retitled June 2026 version.

cards.title: Five of the twelve invited actually turned up
cards.hook: One agent was told she wanted to throw a party. Nobody told anyone else anything.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The agents outranked the humans, and that is the problem
cards.hook: In the believability ranking, the full architecture beat the human-written baseline. That is more troubling than it sounds.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: An agent that remembers everything can act on nothing
cards.hook: An agent that remembers everything is an agent that can act on nothing. The fix is three numbers.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The hard part of a multi-agent simulation is the referee
cards.hook: Dungeons & Dragons solved a problem that multi-agent AI keeps rediscovering: somebody has to say what actually happened.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: A sample drawn from a population that doesn't exist
cards.hook: Give a language model a stranger's biography and it will answer the survey as that stranger. Often correctly.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The benchmark isn't truth. It's you, two weeks later.
cards.hook: How good can a simulated person be? The ceiling is not truth. It is you, answering again two weeks later.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Source repointed to arXiv v1: the unversioned link now serves the retitled June 2026 v3. v1's 1,052 participants, two-hour interviews and 85% figure all confirmed.

cards.title: Two hours of life story, or a questionnaire. Four points apart.
cards.hook: Two hours of life story, or a filled-in questionnaire. The gap between them is four points.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Marked the 100x interview-cost figure as an estimate. 83/82/86 vs 74% and the asymptote wording confirmed verbatim against arXiv:2411.10109v3 (28 June 2026).

cards.title: The means matched. Nothing else did.
cards.hook: The synthetic survey got the means right and the disagreement wrong. Means are not what regressions are made of.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Replaced 'results shifted as the model was updated' with the paper's own claim: the same prompt gave significantly different results three months later.

cards.title: What result would make you abandon your own simulation?
cards.hook: A referee asks one question and the whole project depends on whether you prepared for it.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Whose opinions does the model reflect?
cards.hook: Sixty US demographic groups, one benchmark. The gap between the model and some of them is the size of a partisan divide.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Source titled 'American Trends Panel' pointed at the Pew Research Center page; retitled to match.

cards.title: Ubicar un partido en el eje izquierda-derecha contando palabras
cards.hook: ¿Dónde queda un partido en el eje izquierda-derecha? Hay una respuesta que solo cuenta palabras.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Se anadio la fuente de Wordscores (Laver, Benoit y Garry 2003), que el cuerpo citaba sin respaldo.

cards.title: Lo que Google creía saber de la gripe
cards.hook: Durante dos años Google se adelantó al CDC. Después sobreestimó la gripe en 100 de 108 semanas seguidas de medición.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: El gancho decia '100 semanas seguidas'; Lazer et al. reportan 100 de 108 semanas entre agosto 2011 y septiembre 2013.

cards.title: It was anonymous for about a week
cards.hook: The dataset was anonymised, approved by an ethics board, and identified as one specific university almost immediately.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Sixty-one million people, one button, one day
cards.hook: On one day in 2010, Facebook randomised 61 million Americans and changed who voted.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: 'Close friends mattered four times as much' replaced by the paper's own finding: close friends, 7% of ties, carried essentially all of the contagion.

cards.title: Every model of language is wrong, and some of them are cheap
cards.hook: Every quantitative model of language is wrong. The useful question is which wrongness you can live with.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Fit the text better, understand the topics worse
cards.hook: Tune a topic model to predict text better and humans understand its topics less. That was measured.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Cosimo never said what he wanted. That was the strategy.
cards.hook: The Medici were not the richest family in Florence, nor the best connected. They were the only ones in the middle.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Remember eigenvectors? One of them ranked the entire web
cards.hook: The algorithm that ranked the web is one eigenvector of one matrix, and you already know which one.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Your algorithm will find communities. Even when there are none.
cards.hook: Run the standard algorithm on a graph with no communities at all and it will hand you communities.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Some things need two friends, and that changes the whole picture
cards.hook: A virus needs one carrier. A behaviour often needs two, and that one change reverses everything you know about networks.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Tus amigos tienen más amigos que tú, y no es culpa tuya
cards.hook: No es inseguridad tuya: en casi cualquier red, el amigo promedio es más popular que tú.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: 'Semanas antes' era impreciso: Christakis y Fowler miden 13,9 dias de adelanto del grupo de amigos.

cards.title: The runaway epidemic that was solved by drawing dots
cards.hook: Girls kept running away from the same reform school in waves. A psychiatrist drew the friendships and found why.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Remember Königsberg? Euler got the easy part: someone handed him the edges
cards.hook: Euler got handed the bridges. You have to decide what the edges are, and that decision is the model.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The job came from someone you barely see
cards.hook: Granovetter asked people how they found their job. Only one in six heard it from someone they saw often.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Who do you take out of the network first?
cards.hook: If crime is contagious along friendships, the person to remove is not the busiest criminal.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The exact moment a crowd turns into a society
cards.hook: Add random links to a crowd of strangers and nothing happens, nothing happens, then suddenly everyone is connected.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Scale-free networks are rare
cards.hook: Someone finally tested "scale-free networks are everywhere" on a thousand networks.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked to the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman card, which teaches the same lesson from a different study.

cards.title: Two ingredients, and hubs appear out of nowhere
cards.hook: Random graphs have no hubs. Real ones are full of them, and one extra ingredient explains why.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Rewire one link in a hundred and the world collapses
cards.hook: Rewire one link in a hundred and the world shrinks almost all the way. Nobody loses a single friend.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: The famous six degrees, and the letters that never showed up
cards.hook: "Six degrees of separation" is a real finding from an experiment in which most of the chains never arrived.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Ignore anyone too far from you, and consensus stops being guaranteed
cards.hook: Add one rule to a model that always reaches consensus — ignore people too far from you — and consensus stops being guaranteed.
cards.author: author-css-1

reviewed.notes: Lorenz's first bifurcation is into three clusters, not two camps; rewritten with his own epsilon values (0.3 consensus, 0.19 split).

cards.title: Remember fixed points? Agreement is one of them
cards.hook: Agreement is a point a map doesn't move. That sentence is a theorem, and it comes with a rate.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Nobody persuades anybody, and somebody still wins
cards.hook: Nobody argues, nobody persuades, everyone just averages. Somebody still wins.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: La cámara de eco: la historia es buena, los datos no la acompañan
cards.hook: Todo el mundo sabe que las redes polarizan. La evidencia lleva una década sin cooperar.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Remember Markov chains? Here is one where the answer is known in advance
cards.hook: Copy a random neighbour, forever. Your side's chance of winning was fixed before anybody moved.
cards.author: author-css-1

cards.title: Progresa repartió la ayuda por sorteo, y por eso sabemos si sirvió
cards.hook: En 1997 México repartió un programa social echando suertes entre pueblos. Fue lo más inteligente que hizo.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Stocks beat bonds so badly that holding bonds is the puzzle
cards.hook: Stocks beat bonds by about six points a year for a century. No sane risk aversion explains a gap that big.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Investors sell what is rising and keep what is falling
cards.hook: Investors realise about 14.8% of their winning positions and 9.8% of their losing ones. The tax code says do the opposite.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: PGR/PLR figures attributed to non-December months and December reversal (10.8% vs 12.8%) added, per Odean 1998.

cards.title: Pick a number. Closest to two-thirds of the average wins.
cards.hook: Pick a number from 0 to 100. Closest to two-thirds of the average wins. The equilibrium is 0 and you should not play it.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Nobody plays the equilibrium. Everybody plays the room.
cards.hook: Game theorists who know the equilibrium of the two-thirds game perfectly well still do not play it. They are right not to.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Rationality has two blades, and one of them is the world
cards.hook: Simon's answer to "why are people irrational?" was that you are staring at one blade of a pair of scissors.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Linda is a bank teller, and 85% of people got it wrong
cards.hook: Adding a detail to a story can only make it less likely. About 85% of people bet the other way.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Remember Bayes? Watch what happens when the base rate goes
cards.hook: A witness who is right 80% of the time says the cab was blue. The cab was probably green.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The wheel of fortune was rigged, and it moved every answer
cards.hook: A number produced by a rigged wheel of fortune moved people's estimates by twenty points.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The card dealers did not flinch, and that is the interesting part
cards.hook: The endowment effect showed up in every classroom. Then someone ran it on people who trade for a living.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The mug that was worth twice as much once it was yours
cards.hook: Half a Cornell class got a free mug. Minutes later the mug was worth more than twice what the other half would pay.
cards.author: lead

reviewed.notes: Buyer valuation corrected from about 3.50 to about 3 dollars (KKT 1990 medians are roughly 7 vs 3); hook now says more than twice.

cards.title: Cab drivers quit early on exactly the days they should stay out
cards.hook: On the busiest days, New York cab drivers went home early. Twenty-five years later economists are still arguing about why.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Lose the ticket and you go home. Lose the cash and you watch.
cards.hook: Lose the ticket and 46% buy another. Lose an identical banknote and 88% do.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The brain has no loss centre, which is stranger than having one
cards.hook: If losses hurt twice as much, there should be a pain circuit for them. There is not — and that is the finding.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: El milagro español de los trasplantes no fue la ley
cards.hook: La ley de consentimiento presunto es de 1979. Durante diez años no movió ni una cifra.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: The 2022 donor rate softened to more than 46 pmp: the official ONT figure is 46.03, the cited page rounds it to 47.

cards.title: A nudge is real, and about six times smaller than you read
cards.hook: Same interventions, two literatures: 1.4 percentage points in government trials, 8.7 in the published papers.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Changed to two of the largest US nudge units, per the paper; source title now cites Econometrica 90(1). All figures verified.

cards.title: Austria says yes 99.98% of the time. Germany says yes 12%.
cards.hook: Austria's effective consent to organ donation is 99.98%. Germany's is about 12%. The difference is which box is pre-ticked.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Write down five ranges you are 90% sure about
cards.hook: Five questions, five ranges, 90% confidence each. If you are calibrated you should miss half of one.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: 93% of drivers are in the better half
cards.hook: 93% of American drivers put themselves in the better half. The effect reverses for hard skills.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added Svenson (1981, Acta Psychologica) as the source for the 93% figure.

cards.title: Four boxes that hold almost everything people do about risk
cards.hook: One risk attitude cannot bend twice. The fourfold pattern needs both of prospect theory's moves at once.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Why one person buys lottery tickets and insurance
cards.hook: Buying insurance makes you risk-averse. Buying a lottery ticket makes you risk-seeking. Millions of people do both before lunch.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Two choices, and you have just broken the theory
cards.hook: Two pairs of gambles. Almost everyone answers in a way that no utility function on earth can produce.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: You do not feel wealth. You feel the change.
cards.hook: Your bank balance cannot tell you whether you are happy about your salary. Prospect theory puts that in the arithmetic.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: "I placed too much faith in underpowered studies"
cards.hook: In 2017 Kahneman read a blog post taking apart a chapter of his own book, and agreed with it in public.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Quote verified verbatim; the unverifiable 14 February date dropped from the prose and a Retraction Watch source added.

cards.title: Remember Popper's question? Preregistration is it, in triplicate
cards.hook: Popper's demarcation asks what would refute you. Preregistration is that question turned into paperwork.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The scoreboard, and why it is not an argument for cynicism
cards.hook: Psychology replicated 36% of the time. Experimental economics, 61%. The list of survivors is not the list you would guess.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: Fifteen societies, one game, and no two played it alike
cards.hook: Mean offers in the ultimatum game ran from 26% to 58% across fifteen small-scale societies. None matched the textbook.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added a related link to the Spanish Machiguenga card.

cards.title: Los machiguenga aceptaron casi todo, y eso volteó la pregunta
cards.hook: Dieciséis de veintiuna ofertas estuvieron en o por debajo del 30%. Los machiguenga rechazaron cuatro en total.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Rejection count fixed: Henrich et al. report 16 of 21 offers at or below 30% and four rejections in total, not one. Related link added.

cards.title: Remember Hamilton's rule? Strangers share none of your genes
cards.hook: Hamilton's rule explains why you would die for two brothers. It predicts zero for an anonymous stranger. People give anyway.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added Fehr and Schmidt (1999) as the source for the inequity-aversion function used in the rigor layer.

cards.title: The savings plan that only asks for money you do not have yet
cards.hook: The plan asks for none of the money you have. It asks for a slice of the raise you have not received yet.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: The choice you make for next year is not the one you will make
cards.hook: Same six-month wait, moved three months into the future, and the answer flips. Pigeons do it too.
cards.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

cards.title: "Hardly anyone takes anyone else's data analyses seriously"
cards.hook: The most quoted sentence ever written about applied economics was an insult, and the profession agreed with it.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: The quote is on p. 37, not the opening, and reads data analyses. Restored verbatim from the AER text and extended with the plumed-birds line.

cards.title: The decade economics stopped believing its own regressions
cards.hook: In 1983 an economist told his colleagues that nobody believed anybody's regressions. He was right, and it worked.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Leamer wording fixed (analyses). Deaton and Heckman wrote in a JEL symposium, not the same issue as Angrist-Pischke, which was JEP.

cards.title: The graph theory you already know, with the arrows meaning something
cards.hook: You already know what a path in a directed graph is. Add one rule about arrowheads and you get a recipe for what to control for.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: It worked in Kenya. Would it work in Boyacá?
cards.hook: A clean, replicated, cheap result from western Kenya. Your job is to say what has to be true before it travels to Boyacá.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: Remember random forests? Now grow one that predicts an effect
cards.hook: A forest predicts an outcome you can see. Point the same machinery at a quantity nobody ever observes and it still works — with one fix.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: The number nobody has ever seen
cards.hook: Every causal claim is about a subtraction where one of the two numbers has never existed.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: The first natural experiment was a fight between two water companies
cards.hook: The famous pump-handle map is the worse study. Snow's masterpiece was a price war between two water companies.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: 420 is the outbreak total, not the toll before the handle came off on 8 September. Snow quote and the 14x ratio verified against the sources.

cards.title: People who go to hospital die more. Subtract carefully.
cards.hook: Sick people go to hospital and hospital patients die more often. The arithmetic of that mistake is two terms long.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: Why the good-looking ones can't act
cards.hook: Looks and talent can be unrelated in the world and still be negatively related among people who got cast.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Removed an Ellenberg essay attribution the cited source does not support; replaced that source with the collider article.

cards.title: The equation stops being true the moment you use it
cards.hook: Your coefficients summarise how people behaved under the old rules. Change the rules and you have invalidated your own regression.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

cards.title: Remember Bayes as a rule for changing your mind? Now do it to a coefficient
cards.hook: Point the rule for changing your mind at a coefficient, and a shrunken estimate stops being a compromise and becomes a posterior.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Minnesota-prior source authors corrected to Doan, Litterman and Sims (1984) per Crossref.

cards.title: A state line, a wage rise, and the most argued-about study in economics
cards.hook: In 1992 New Jersey raised its minimum wage and Pennsylvania did not. Two economists treated a state line as an experiment.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Card-Krueger 2000 reply title corrected against Crossref (A Case Study).

cards.title: Five percent was a convenience, not a discovery
cards.hook: The line between a discovery and a nothing has been 0.05 for a century because one statistician found it handy.
cards.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Usual and convenient is from The Design of Experiments (1935), not the 1920s; Fisher drew the 5 per cent line in 1925. Quote, dates and sources fixed.

cards.title: The laws that never happened, and their significant effects
